title: Inorganic Elements and Compounds
lines: This is the largest chemistry topic, and most questions test whether you remember a reaction, a colour or a use. Learn each element as a chain from the element to its oxide, base or acid and salts. Equations below are balanced; write the conditions (heat, catalyst) as words when you revise.
## Sodium and its compounds
- Sodium is soft, silvery, less dense than water and stored under kerosene. It burns with a yellow flame.
- 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (room temperature, white); 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂ (heating, pale yellow).
- 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑: floats, melts into a ball, moves about, fizzes; the solution turns phenolphthalein red.
- Sodium peroxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂↑ and 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂ (used for oxygen in submarines). In each, 2 mol Na₂O₂ transfers 2 mol electrons.
- Na₂CO₃ versus NaHCO₃: both are alkaline; NaHCO₃ decomposes on heating, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑, while Na₂CO₃ does not. NaHCO₃ reacts faster with acid. Na₂CO₃ is more soluble.
- Conversions: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃; NaHCO₃ + NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
! Trap: sodium added to CuSO₄ solution does not displace copper. It reacts with water first, then NaOH gives blue Cu(OH)₂ precipitate.
> Example: Dropping HCl slowly into Na₂CO₃ solution: when does gas appear?
> First CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻ (no gas). Only after all carbonate becomes hydrogencarbonate does HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂↑ begin. Adding the solution the other way round gives gas immediately.
## Magnesium and aluminium
- Mg burns with a dazzling white light: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; it even burns in CO₂: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C.
- Aluminium is protected by a thin, dense Al₂O₃ layer, so it resists corrosion. It is passivated by cold concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.
- Al reacts with both acid and strong base: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂↑ and 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂↑. Equal masses of Al give equal H₂ with excess of either.
- Thermite reaction: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (high temperature), used to weld rails.
## Amphoteric behaviour
- Al₂O₃ and Al(OH)₃ react with both acids and strong bases:
- Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl → AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al(OH)₃ + NaOH → NaAlO₂ + 2H₂O.
- Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O.
- Lab preparation of Al(OH)₃ uses aluminium salt plus ammonia water, because excess NH₃·H₂O does not dissolve the precipitate: Al³⁺ + 3NH₃·H₂O → Al(OH)₃↓ + 3NH₄⁺.
- Other substances that react with both acid and base: NaHCO₃, (NH₄)₂CO₃, amino acids, and Al itself (but Al is a metal, not an amphoteric compound).
> Example: NaOH solution is added drop by drop to AlCl₃ until in excess. What is seen?
> A white precipitate forms (Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓), grows to a maximum, then dissolves as Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → AlO₂⁻ + 2H₂O. The mole ratio of NaOH used in the two stages is 3 : 1.
## Iron and its compounds
- Iron reacts with Cl₂ to give FeCl₃ (strong oxidant) but with S or HCl to give Fe(II): 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃; Fe + S → FeS; Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂↑.
- With steam at high temperature: 3Fe + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂.
- Oxides: FeO black, Fe₂O₃ red-brown (rust, red pigment), Fe₃O₄ black and magnetic.
- Hydroxides: Fe(OH)₂ is white, quickly turning grey-green then red-brown in air: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃. Fe(OH)₃ is a red-brown precipitate.
- Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺: 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺: 2FeCl₃ + Fe → 3FeCl₂ (iron powder keeps Fe²⁺ solutions from oxidising); 2FeCl₃ + Cu → 2FeCl₂ + CuCl₂ (etching circuit boards).
- Fe²⁺ solutions are pale green; Fe³⁺ solutions are yellow to brown. KSCN turns Fe³⁺ blood-red.
! Trap: the reaction of FeCl₃ with Cu does not mean iron is less active than copper. It is Fe³⁺, a strong oxidant, that attacks Cu; the product is Fe²⁺, not Fe.
## Copper and its compounds
- Copper does not react with dilute HCl or dilute H₂SO₄. It reacts with oxidising acids:
- Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc.) → CuSO₄ + SO₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat).
- Cu + 4HNO₃(conc.) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂↑ + 2H₂O; 3Cu + 8HNO₃(dilute) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO↑ + 4H₂O.
- Green patina: Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃ (basic copper carbonate). CuO black, Cu₂O red, Cu(OH)₂ blue precipitate, CuSO₄ white (anhydrous), CuSO₄·5H₂O blue.
> Example: In 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, what fraction of HNO₃ acts as oxidising agent?
> Only the 2 N atoms that become NO are reduced, so 2 of 8, i.e. 1/4. The other 6 act as an acid (they stay as nitrate).
## Chlorine
- Cl₂ is a yellow-green, toxic, dense gas. It is a strong oxidising agent.
- 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (white smoke); Cu + Cl₂ → CuCl₂ (brown-yellow smoke); H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (pale flame, or explosion in light).

- With water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. HClO is a weak acid, a strong oxidant and bleach, and decomposes in light: 2HClO → 2HCl + O₂↑. So fresh chlorine water bleaches; old chlorine water is just dilute HCl.
- With bases: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (bleach); 2Cl₂ + 2Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + Ca(ClO)₂ + 2H₂O (bleaching powder, active part Ca(ClO)₂).
- Halogen displacement: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (I₂ turns starch blue); oxidising power Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
! Trap: dry chlorine does not bleach dry coloured cloth; the bleaching agent is HClO, which needs water.
## Sulfur
- S + O₂ → SO₂ (blue-violet flame in O₂). SO₂ is a colourless, choking gas, an acidic oxide: SO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₃.

- SO₂ bleaches by combining with coloured substances (reversible: heating restores the colour of decolourised magenta). It also acts as a reducing agent: SO₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O → H₂SO₄ + 2HCl, so mixing SO₂ and Cl₂ in equal moles removes bleaching power. SO₂ decolourises acidified KMnO₄ by reduction, not bleaching.
- 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (catalyst, heat). SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

- Concentrated H₂SO₄: dehydrating (chars sugar), hygroscopic (drying agent for acidic and neutral gases), strong oxidant (reacts with Cu and C when hot: C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂↑ + 2SO₂↑ + 2H₂O). It passivates Fe and Al in the cold.
! Trap: concentrated H₂SO₄ cannot dry NH₃ (basic) or H₂S and HI (reducing). Dilution: always pour acid slowly into water while stirring.
## Nitrogen
- N₂ is very unreactive because of its N≡N triple bond. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (lightning). 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (red-brown). 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO.
- Ammonia: very soluble (fountain experiment), solution is weakly alkaline: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃·H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (white smoke).
- Catalytic oxidation: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt catalyst, heat), the first step in making nitric acid.
- Ammonium salts decompose on heating (NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl, recombining when cool) and release NH₃ with bases.
- Nitric acid is a strong oxidant at any concentration; it does not release H₂ with metals. Concentrated HNO₃ decomposes in light (stored in brown bottles): 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ + 2H₂O.
## Carbon and silicon
- C: CO₂ is an acidic oxide; CO is toxic (binds haemoglobin) and a reducing agent. CO₂ + C → 2CO (high temperature).
- CO₂ into limewater: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O (cloudy); excess CO₂ clears it: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂.
- Silicon is a semiconductor (chips, solar cells). SiO₂ forms optical fibres, quartz and sand.
- SiO₂ is acidic but does not react with water. SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O (so NaOH bottles use rubber stoppers, not glass). SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄↑ + 2H₂O (HF etches glass).
- Silicic acid is weaker than carbonic acid: Na₂SiO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → H₂SiO₃↓ + Na₂CO₃.
- Silicate materials: glass, cement, ceramics.
## Acids, bases and salts in general
- Acid + metal (more active than H) → salt + H₂. Acid + basic oxide or base → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
- A stronger acid makes a weaker acid from its salt: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑.
- Insoluble in water: most carbonates (except Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺), BaSO₄, AgCl, Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Fe(OH)₃, Cu(OH)₂, CaCO₃. All nitrates and all Na⁺, K⁺ and NH₄⁺ salts are soluble.
## Everyday and environmental chemistry
- Acid rain (pH < 5.6) comes from SO₂ (coal burning) and NOₓ (car exhausts). Desulfurisation: add CaO to coal so 2CaO + 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄.
- Photochemical smog: NOₓ and hydrocarbons in sunlight. Ozone layer damage: CFCs (freons). Greenhouse effect: CO₂ and CH₄. Eutrophication: phosphates and nitrates in water. White pollution: plastics.

- Uses: NaHCO₃ in baking and antacids; Al(OH)₃ antacid; Fe₂O₃ red paint; NaClO and ClO₂ disinfectants; alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O purifies water (Al(OH)₃ colloid adsorbs dirt) but does not disinfect; N₂ as a protective gas; liquid NH₃ as a refrigerant.
